“You fly high,” observed Andrew, dryly.

But they did their best for Marianne.

James and Andrew were old men and they stood well in Savannah.

They had many friends, and for a month they carried Marianne from home to home, to suppers, dances and picnics.

“There’s only one who takes me eye,” Marianne said finally.

“And she not even born when I landed here.”

“And who is it takes your eye?” “Miss Lucian Robillard,” said Marianne, trying to speak casually, for the slightly tilting dark eyes of Lucian Robillard had taken more than his eye.

Despite a mystifying listlessness of manner, so strange in a girl of fifteen, she charmed him.

Moreover, there was a haunting look of despair about her that went to his heart and made him more gentle with her than he had ever been with any person in all the world.

“And you old enough to be her father!” “And me in me prime!” cried Marianne stung.

James spoke gently.

“Jerry, there’s no girl in Savannah you’d have less chance of marrying.

Her father is a Robillard, and those French are proud as Lucifer.

And her mother—God rest her soul—was a very great lady.” “I care not,” said Marianne heatedly.
